newsitem.title: USA: Clinton reiterates opposition to late-term abortion.
newsitem.headline: Clinton reiterates opposition to late-term abortion.

text.p: President Clinton Friday reiterated his opposition to a bill banning certain late-term abortions, saying he would not sign it unless Congress allowed exceptions to protect a woman's health.

Clinton earlier this year vetoed a similar abortion bill. The House overrode Clinton's veto, but bill supporters failed to failed to muster the necessary two-thirds majority for an override in the Senate.
An emotional Clinton told a White House news conference Friday he had long opposed most third trimester abortions.

But he said he had a responsibility to protect women who discovered late in wanted pregnancies they were carrying a badly deformed foetus or faced a health risk of their own. Clinton called the procedure the best option for ensuring such women could bear children in the future.

"Hillary and I -- we only had one child. And I just cannot look at a woman who's in a situation where the baby she is bearing, against all her wishes and prayers, is going to die anyway, and tell her that I am signing a law which will prevent her from ever having another child," he said.
Clinton said bill supporters had ignored his pleas to allow the procedure when a woman's health was at risk. The bill contained an exception when a woman's life was in danger.
"They would not do it, I believe, because it was great politics," Clinton said. "If they will help me with language here and do it in good faith, I will happily sign this bill."

The National Right to Life Committee sharply criticised Clinton. In a statement the group said most of the contested abortions took place in the fifth and sixth months of pregnancy, not the third trimester.

"President Clinton's proposal ... thus would allow the continuation of thousands of partial-birth abortions on healthy babies of healthy mothers," said Right to Life Legislative Director Douglas Johnson.
"Partial birth" abortion, technically known as intact dilation and evacuation, is sometimes used in second and third trimester abortions.
Bill supporters assert there is no medical reason to ever use the procedure. They contend it is used in cases where there is no health problem with the foetus or the woman.
Further, abortion opponents say past health exceptions have been interpreted too broadly, allowing abortions to take place due to emotional distress or the youth of a woman.
Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle has also said he wants to work out a compromise bill to bar third trimester abortions, with exceptions for a mother's life and health.
According to the Alan Guttmacher Institute, 89 percent of the 1.5 million U.S. abortions each year take place in the first trimester of pregnancy.
